title: Emotional-Intelligence Claims Laboratory
summary: Self-report emotional intelligence overlaps a personality questionnaire; ability emotional intelligence overlaps a reasoning test. See both overlaps in one picture, then ask whether either measure predicts anything beyond them.
learningObjectives: State what a self-report emotional-intelligence scale and an ability measure each overlap with among established constructs.
Explain why two measures sharing a label are not thereby measures of the same thing.
Say what incremental validity asks that a raw correlation with an outcome does not.
Judge a marketing claim about a psychological measure against the evidence a correlation could support.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every correlation and regression runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it and produces no score for them.
accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, radios, checkboxes, a select and buttons throughout; every slider announces what it controls in words rather than as a bare number. The correlation matrix is an ordinary table whose cells state their correlation as a number and whose row headers name the collection method, so the tint and the dotted underline marking same-method pairs are reading aids rather than the only cue. Judged claims state agreement in words as well as by border colour. Reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths. Step 1 shows one slider and one result: three overlap rows, each stating its relationship in words and its correlation as a figure, with the bar itself aria-hidden so no information rests on it. The contrast row is hatched as well as tinted and named as a contrast in its label. The full matrix and the two method sliders sit inside native <details> elements, keyboard reachable in one step and announced as collapsed rather than disabled.
readmeTopic: Construct validity: convergent, discriminant and incremental evidence, and what an attractive label can hide
simulationNotes: Six fictional measures described by method type rather than by name. No published emotional-intelligence questionnaire, task, item or scoring key is reproduced, quoted, paraphrased or scored, and no specific test is criticised. Correlations are model-implied: each measure is a weighted sum of independent sources - dispositional, emotion ability, general cognitive, a questionnaire method effect and a testing method effect - so the correlation between two measures is the sum of the products of their shared coefficients. Standardised regression weights are solved from that matrix by Gaussian elimination and the variance accounted for is reported from them. The self-report scale's content is a fixed amount of common variance split between two sources by one angle, so the mix slider redirects the scale without improving it. The numbers are chosen to make a teaching pattern visible and are not estimates of any published finding.
